solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Trader Mike in predicament with church spreading bombast (5,8)

indicators.note: Mike goes inside the predicament
the bombast is spread apart to make room for the church

blocks.note: a scrape = a predicament
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet, set inside SCRAPE: SCRAP(M)E
rant = bombastic talk
standard abbreviation, set inside RANT: R(CH)ANT

annotation.surface: A dealer called Mike is in trouble with a church that is full of hot air.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spreading' reads as the church spreading its message, but it means the bombast is pulled apart so the church can sit inside it.
annotation.definitionFit: A scrap merchant is a trader who buys and sells scrap.

entries.clue: Complaint from south Taipei came unexpectedly (11)

indicators.note: the letters turn up in an unexpected order

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: Someone lodges a complaint after a trip south to Taipei came as a surprise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grievance, but it means an illness, as in 'a stomach complaint'.
annotation.definitionFit: Septicaemia is blood poisoning, a serious medical complaint.

entries.clue: Verse in song of praise briefly adopted by army corps (5)

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its last letter
the corps takes the shortened hymn in, as a family adopts a child

blocks.note: RE = Royal Engineers, the army corps
a hymn is a song of praise; 'briefly' docks its last letter, and the rest goes inside RE

annotation.surface: An army corps takes up a hymn, verse and all.
annotation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers (RE) are the crossword's usual army corps.
annotation.definitionFit: Rhyme can mean verse in general, as in 'nursery rhyme'.

entries.clue: Seemingly ceaseless repeat Rumpole regularly broadcast (9)

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so the letters are taken at a steady every-other step
the letters are scattered widely, like seed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, used as it stands
the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of rUmPoLe

annotation.surface: A TV repeat of Rumpole of the Bailey seems to be on forever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the TV picture so well that it hides its job of mixing the letters. Rumpole of the Bailey is a long-running British TV legal drama.
annotation.definitionFit: Something perpetual goes on, or seems to go on, without end.

entries.clue: European going on vacation with only half of blasted drink (3,4)

indicators.note: the word is emptied, keeping only its outside letters
keep just the first half of the word

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
GoinG with its middle vacated
FLIPPING (= blasted, a mild curse) cut to its first half

annotation.surface: A European heads off on holiday having had only half of a drink that blew him away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blasted' is a mild British curse, like 'flipping'. 'On vacation' is a common way of saying 'emptied'.
annotation.definitionFit: Egg flip is a drink of beaten egg with milk or alcohol, like eggnog.

entries.clue: Clergy unwilling to be led by agnostic’s conclusion (5)

indicators.note: a word's conclusion is where it ends, so only its final letter is used
the last letter goes in front

blocks.note: last letter of agnostiC
loth = unwilling, a variant of loath

annotation.surface: Clergy are reluctant to follow the lead of an agnostic's reasoning.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts clergy and an agnostic at odds, which keeps 'the cloth' out of mind.
annotation.definitionFit: 'The cloth' is the clergy, from their distinctive dress.

entries.clue: Complain bitterly about being shown up following software evaluation (9)

indicators.note: the complaint wraps around the next piece
in a down answer, the piece reads upwards
the rest comes after the software

blocks.note: an app is a piece of software
to rail = to complain bitterly
AS (= being, as in 'as a child') turned upwards, set inside RAIL: RAI(SA)L

annotation.surface: Someone moans after a software review made them look bad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Being' stands for AS ('as / being a child, I…'), and 'shown up' looks like embarrassment but turns it round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a staff appraisal is a formal evaluation of someone's work.

entries.clue: Cask enthusiast rolled over (3)

indicators.note: the word is turned over, reading backwards

blocks.note: a nut = a fan, as in 'fitness nut'

annotation.surface: A beer lover's barrel is rolled across the cellar floor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rolled over' suits a barrel, which is what the answer is.
annotation.definitionFit: A tun is a large cask for wine or beer.

entries.clue: Nimble mole checking run (4)

indicators.note: the mole holds back, and so holds in, the run

blocks.note: a mole is a spy inside an organisation
cricket scoring abbreviation, which goes inside the mole's letters

annotation.surface: A quick-footed mole stops someone making a run for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mole' is the burrowing animal in the surface and the planted spy in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Spry means nimble and lively, especially of an older person.

entries.clue: Post-defeat, again rallying Germany about call involving press (10)

indicators.note: Germany's abbreviation is turned about
the call wraps around the press

blocks.note: abbreviation for Germany
to ring = to call on the phone
Oxford University Press, set inside RING: R(OUP)ING

annotation.surface: After a loss, Germany's side regroups around a rallying call, with the press involved.
annotation.walkthrough: OUP is Oxford University Press, a publisher the Times uses as 'press'.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: an army that regroups gathers its scattered forces to rally after a setback.

entries.clue: Coveted property pair has left in excellent Suffolk village (8)

indicators.note: the pair's letters depart from the word
what remains goes inside the next word

blocks.note: swell = excellent, old-fashioned slang
PRIZE (something coveted) minus PR (pair); the remainder sits inside the word for excellent

annotation.surface: An estate agent's advert: a sought-after house in a lovely village, the couple having moved out.
annotation.walkthrough: Sizewell is a Suffolk coastal village known for its nuclear power stations. PR is the usual abbreviation for pair.
annotation.definitionFit: Sizewell is a village on the Suffolk coast in eastern England.

entries.clue: Tries ecstasy, the ultimate transport for some? (6)

blocks.note: a court hears, that is tries, a case
E = the drug ecstasy

annotation.surface: Someone tries ecstasy, as the ultimate trip for some partygoers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ultimate' is the joke: a hearse is the final vehicle anyone rides in. The question mark flags that the definition is playful.
annotation.definitionFit: A hearse is the last vehicle many of us will ride in.

entries.clue: Novel form of alarm sirens (5,6)

indicators.note: the letters take a new form

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: A new kind of alarm siren has been invented.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as the adjective 'new', but it is the noun: a book.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: George Eliot's 1861 book about a miserly weaver is one novel among many.

entries.clue: Notorious meal in most unsuitable boozer (4,6)

blocks.note: the last = the least suitable, as in 'the last person I'd ask'
one who sups, that is drinks

annotation.surface: A dreadful meal is served in the worst pub imaginable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, which the surface uses, but here it is a drinker: one who sups.
annotation.definitionFit: The Last Supper, Jesus's final meal with his disciples, is the most famous meal in history.

entries.clue: Four-letter word, eg “tart”, deplorably supported by beastly male (9)

indicators.note: the letters are treated badly, that is mixed up
in a down answer, the ram sits below and holds it up

blocks.note: EG TART rearranged
a ram is a male sheep

annotation.surface: A dictionary entry notes that 'tart' is a four-letter word, one used rudely by a brute of a man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tart' is indeed a four-letter word, and a mildly rude one, which makes the definition feel like part of the example. 'Beastly' just means 'of a beast'.
annotation.definitionFit: From Greek tetra (four) and gramma (letter): the technical term for any word written with four letters.

entries.clue: Trots round public leisure area with yellow covers? (2-7)

indicators.note: the Trots go round the rest
the yellow joins the leisure area

blocks.note: Trotskyists, left-wingers, are reds
the rec, a recreation ground, set inside REDS
or = gold/yellow in heraldry; it follows the rec inside the Trots

annotation.surface: Joggers run round a park wearing yellow waterproofs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Covers' looks like the joggers' clothing; it is songs another artist records again. A rec is British for a public playing field.
annotation.definitionFit: A band that covers a song re-records it in its own version.

entries.clue: Leaving hotel, family lying about identity (4)

indicators.note: the hotel is left behind, so its letter departs from the word
what remains lies the other way round

blocks.note: FLESH (as in 'flesh and blood', family) without H for hotel

annotation.surface: A family skips out on a hotel bill after lying about who they are.
annotation.walkthrough: H is Hotel in the NATO alphabet. 'Lying about' reads as dishonesty but turns the letters round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: your sense of self is your sense of who you are.

entries.clue: Initially Sweep, a dog, snubbed Sooty? This could be so (4)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition works as a description: smut is what could make something sooty

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the word's opening letter is used
the dog's name is cut short, like a snub nose

blocks.note: first letter of Sweep
MUTT (a mongrel) with its last letter docked

annotation.surface: Sweep, the dog puppet, cold-shoulders his partner Sooty.
annotation.walkthrough: Sooty and Sweep are a British children's TV glove-puppet bear and dog, so the surface is a puppet quarrel. Smut is soot or a sooty smudge.
annotation.definitionFit: Smut is a flake of soot, the thing that makes something sooty.

entries.clue: Vulgar, lawless half of crowd’s rioting (5-5)

indicators.note: keep only the first half of the word
a rioting crowd is in disorder, and so are these letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, used as it stands
the first three letters of CROWDS

annotation.surface: A rough, lawless part of the crowd is rioting.
annotation.walkthrough: Take half of CROWDS, with its 's, not of CROWD, to get three whole letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Lower-class is used, snobbishly, to mean vulgar or common.

entries.clue: Perhaps one who quickly moves a tiny distance (7)

blocks.note: one who whisks things away, a made-up agent noun
the tiny margin by which a race is won

annotation.surface: Someone darting about only ever covers a short distance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns that WHISKER as 'one who whisks' is a whimsical coinage, not a dictionary sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A whisker is a very small margin, and a whisker is also someone who whisks.

entries.clue: Bears receiving treats every so often as bait (6)

indicators.note: the word takes the letters in
take letters at intervals

blocks.note: has = bears, as in 'bears a name'
the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of tReAtS, received inside the word for bears

annotation.surface: Bears are lured with treats scattered about as bait.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals being tempted; it is the verb. 'Bait' is the verb too: to torment.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from bear-baiting: setting dogs on a chained bear to torment it.

entries.clue: Delivered fine cut (5)

indicators.note: the word is spoken, as a speech is delivered

blocks.note: sheer = fine, as of a thin fabric

annotation.surface: A fine cut of meat has been delivered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' looks like a courier's word, but it means spoken.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, most familiar from sheep being sheared of their fleece.

entries.clue: Gradually winch me aloft, but not to the full extent (8)

indicators.text: but not to the full extent
indicators.note: only part of the words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, dropping the first and last two

annotation.surface: Someone asks to be hoisted up slowly, and not all the way.
annotation.walkthrough: Inchmeal is an old word meaning 'inch by inch'. The surface of being winched up slowly fits the definition exactly.
annotation.definitionFit: Inchmeal means gradually, little by little.

entries.clue: Fighter protects revolutionary British gangland boss, say (2,3)

indicators.note: the fighter surrounds, guarding, the letters
the abbreviation is turned round

blocks.note: a MiG is a Russian fighter plane
BR (British) turned round, then protected inside the fighter

annotation.surface: A hired fighter guards a British revolutionary.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a noun for a rebel; it is an adjective saying 'turn this round'.
annotation.definitionFit: Mr Big is the nickname for the head of a criminal gang.

entries.clue: RIP, weightlifter? Sentimental stuff (4-6)

blocks.note: a rip = a tear
one who lifts a weight with the jerk, as in the clean and jerk

annotation.surface: A gravestone for a weightlifter, the kind of thing that brings on a sob.
annotation.walkthrough: RIP is capitalised to suggest 'rest in peace' and a death; in the wordplay it is just a rip.
annotation.definitionFit: A tear-jerker is a sentimental film or story made to make you cry.

entries.clue: Journalist bagging last of lion’s share (3)

indicators.note: the journalist puts the letter in a bag, that is contains it
the last of anything is its final part, here the final letter of the word

blocks.note: ED = editor
last letter of lioN, bagged by the journalist

annotation.surface: A reporter grabs the lion's share of the credit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lion's share' is a set phrase that pulls 'share' into the wordplay; it is the definition. One's end of a deal is one's share.
annotation.definitionFit: Your end of a deal is your share of it, as in 'keep up your end'.

entries.clue: Live next-door to new unknown engineer (4)

blocks.note: to be = to live, exist
standard abbreviation
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

annotation.surface: Someone lives next door to a mysterious new engineer.
annotation.walkthrough: Karl Benz was the German engineer who built the first practical motor car.
annotation.definitionFit: Karl Benz was a German automotive engineer.

entries.clue: UK business magnate having previously made rare volatile crystalline product (8,5)

indicators.note: the anagram comes before the magnate
the letters are unstable and shift

blocks.note: MADE RARE rearranged
Alan Sugar, founder of Amstrad and host of the UK Apprentice

annotation.surface: A British tycoon made his fortune from a rare, unstable crystal.
annotation.walkthrough: Alan Sugar is a British businessman famous from TV's The Apprentice. 'Volatile' and 'crystalline' borrow chemistry words to hide the kitchen.
annotation.definitionFit: Demerara sugar is a light brown sugar with large crystals.
